\begin{abstract}
Standard confusion-matrix correction for noisy annotations assumes uniform error rates.
When this assumption fails---as it routinely does with LLM classifiers, whose error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across subgroups---correction can reverse the sign of estimated causal effects, concluding a beneficial treatment is harmful.
We derive an exact bias identity for this setting: global correction introduces subgroup-level bias with a product form $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, factoring into each subgroup's deviation from the pooled error rate, the treatment effect heterogeneity, and an amplification factor from matrix inversion.
This population-level identity---verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ across synthetic grids, semi-synthetic evaluations using 11 empirical LLM confusion matrices, and three structurally distinct CATE estimators---predicts that global correction reverses CATE sign in 14.9\% of configurations at $\tau(0) = 0.03$ and amplifies bias in all eight real LLMs tested.
The identity yields a diagnostic: a condition on per-subgroup error rates alone predicts when correction increases bias, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero $\Delta\tau$; $0.86$ across all synthetic subgroups; $0.63$ on real LLM error profiles).
The per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity reduces $|\text{bias}|$ by $7.4\times$ via hierarchical Bayesian estimation; when error heterogeneity is insufficient, the diagnostic alone guides practitioners to retain global correction.
\end{abstract}

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Per-subgroup correction requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ expert labels per subgroup and moderate classifier accuracy ($\text{FPR}_s, \text{FNR}_s < 0.5$); below these thresholds, stratification incurs more variance than the bias it removes.
At $K{=}8$ with $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ (${\approx}31$ labels/subgroup), coverage remains nominal ($\geq$95.6\%) but RMSE exceeds global correction, establishing a scalability boundary under fixed expert budget (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).
The diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) achieves AUC $= 0.86$ on synthetic data but degrades to $0.63$ on real LLM confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:screening}); it should be paired with $R^2$ validation of the bias identity rather than used as a standalone rule.

Assumption~(A1)---conditional independence of misclassification and potential outcomes---is not empirically testable.
Sensitivity analysis shows robustness up to $\gamma = 0.2$ for outcome-dependent misclassification (coverage $\geq$93.5\%; Appendix~\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}) and $\gamma_T \leq 0.05$ for treatment-dependent misclassification (coverage $\geq$89.7\%; Appendix~\ref{app:treatment_dep}).

The method requires discrete, pre-specified subgroups; continuous effect modifiers require discretization, and data-driven subgroup discovery risks overfitting.
Ground-truth subgroup CATEs are unavailable in public datasets---classic causal inference benchmarks lack the LLM annotation step that creates the measurement error we address---so we use synthetic CATE injection on real text features and real LLM annotations (Appendices~\ref{app:dgp},~\ref{app:multilm}).
Code and data generation scripts will be released upon acceptance.
